title: Approximate collective scheduling and link-variance playbook
body:
Summary:

This note captures an exploratory set of experiments and operational heuristics for "approximate collective scheduling" — a lightweight scheduler that intentionally staggers or relaxes strict collective start alignment to reduce tail latency caused by link variance, NIC jitter, and microbursts on NVLink/NVSwitch networks. The goal: actionable playbook for SRE/Runtime teams to test and (optionally) roll out in Dedicated clusters that have mixed topology or noisy neighbor interference.

Why this came up:
- Multiple recent incidents where p99 generation latency spiked even though median throughput and GPU occupancy looked fine.
- Traces pointed to occasional slow allreduce/allgather startup for particular ranks (usually 1 of 8) which then delayed the whole pipeline due to sync points.
- Hypothesis: small link-level jitter (PCIe staging, NVLink transient noise, NIC interrupt coalescing) + strict collective synchronization amplifies tail effect for TP/PP pipelined inference.

Experiment goals:
1) Quantify sensitivity of pipelined/tensor-parallel workloads to per-rank start-time jitter.
2) Measure p50/p90/p99 impact of introducing bounded start-time relaxation (approximate scheduling).
3) Validate interaction with NCCL P2P fallback and different NCCL_ALGO settings.
4) Produce a conservative rollout checklist and safe default params for Dedicated clusters.

Testbed and workload:
- Hardware: 8x A100 80GB connected in a DGX-ish rack pattern (2 NVSwitch domains of 4 GPUs), plus a mixed host PCIe fabric test (one host intentionally over-subscribed).
- Software: Ubuntu 20.04, CUDA 11.8, cuDNN 8.x, NCCL 2.14.3, serving-runtime v0.9.6-dev branch.
- Model: 7B dense transformer (sequence length 2048), KV cache enabled, batch size distribution: 60% single-token interactive, 30% small-context (<=64), 10% long context (>=1024) synthetic generator to emulate real traffic mix.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 token latency, allreduce startup time per-rank (micros), link error/retries from dmesg/NCCL logs, GPU occupancy, host CPU steal/irq counts.
- Baseline: fully synchronized collectives (current runtime behavior).

Experiment variants:
A) Baseline: sync start. Collect traces for baseline distribution across 50k requests.
B) Soft-start window: allow each rank to join the collective in a [-w, +w] microsecond window where w is 0, 50, 200, 500, 2000 us. Implementation: lightweight barrier with randomized backoff seeded by host-id to avoid correlated starts.
C) Priority lanes: allow ranks on same NVSwitch domain to start ahead (inter-domain ranks delayed by d microseconds).
D) NCCL tuning: run B with NCCL_ALGO=Ring and NCCL_ALGO=Tree and NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME variations.
E) P2P fallback stress: artificially drop NVLink packets via driver debug knobs to force P2P fallback and see interaction with soft-start window.

Key commands (how to reproduce quickly):
- Serving runtime client harness: tools/loadgen.py --model=7B-kv --seq=2048 --dist=mixture --qps=120 --duration=30m --trace=collectives.json
- Start runtime with soft-start enabled (local dev flag): RUNTIME_APPROX_COLL_START=1 RUNTIME_COLL_WINDOW_US=200 ./bin/serve --config conf/dedicated-small.json
- NCCL debug: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0 NCCL_ALGO=Ring

Preliminary observations (short):
- Baseline p99: 365 ms per token (confirms prior dashboards). p90: 24 ms. p50: 15 ms.
- Soft-start w=200us: p99 reduced from 365 ms -> 180 ms (roughly half). p90 unchanged. Median unaffected.
- Soft-start w=2000us: p99 improved slightly further but p95/p90 began to drift up for long-context batches (due to extra slack causing queuing).
- Priority lanes (intra-switch start lead of 100us): helped in topologies where NVSwitch locality was dominant; but when traffic crossed domains, improvement was uneven and introduced jitter for those cross-domain batches.
- NCCL_ALGO=Tree had better p99 in some runs but increased average allreduce time for small groups; algorithm choice must be workload-aware.
- Induced P2P fallback: when P2P fallback was triggered, soft-start helped reduce cascading stalls — likely by avoiding simultaneous retries across ranks.

Detailed trace notes:
- Example trace snippet (collectives.json) shows rank 3 startup delayed by 1.2 ms for 23 events out of 50k: driver reported transient DMA stall on host 2. Those 23 events correspond to p99 spikes in baseline.
- With w=200us, those same events showed the slow rank still slow but other ranks had already progressed so wall-clock token time reduced (work continued while one rank caught up).

Operational heuristics (draft playbook):
1) Default rollout for Dedicated clusters: enable RUNTIME_APPROX_COLL_START with COLL_WINDOW_US=200 and COLL_MAX_SLACK_MS=2.0. Conservative because 200us showed large wins without impacting median.
2) Telemetry: emit per-collective start timestamps and per-rank latency histograms to Console for 72-hour burn-in. Add automated alert if p90 latency increases >10% after enabling.
3) Topology-aware tuning: for clusters with well-known NVSwitch partitions (single-domain serving pools), set intra-domain lead=50-150us, inter-domain slack=200-500us.
4) NCCL policy: prefer NCCL_ALGO=Auto in general; but for long-context jobs heavy on large allreduce/tree patterns, prefer Tree; provide a flag to override per-route.
5) Safety fallback: if error rate (NCCL errors or driver dmesg critical) > 0.1% during burn-in, revert and open an incident for deeper root-cause.

Risks and unknowns:
- Approximate start introduces potential for increased memory footprint on ranks that proceed early and buffer more tokens while slow ranks catch up. Need to monitor GPU memory headroom on long-context jobs.
- Interaction with KV cache eviction: if some ranks progress and produce outputs, replaying or reconciling KV cache offsets might be required for correctness (model should be tolerant but double-check for custom kernels).
- Determinism: slight scheduling variance can make debugging replay harder. Add deterministic toggle for perf regression tests.

Open TODOs / next experiments:
- Run same sweep on a 16-GPU job spanning two hosts with different NUMA/PCIe layouts (to evaluate host staging contribution).
- Measure memory amplification for long-context (>4096) when slack is introduced.
- Test interaction with runtime's request demuxing (interleaved batches) and with client-side streaming backpressure.
- Try combining soft-start with microbatch fusion (we saw hints of synergy in one run).
- Run A/B in production for a single customer pool for 48 hours behind a feature flag.

Quick notes for engineers who will pick this up:
- File to look at: runtime/scheduler/approx_coll_start.cc (WIP stub) and runtime/telemetry/coll_metrics.proto.
- Important flags: RUNTIME_APPROX_COLL_START, RUNTIME_COLL_WINDOW_US, RUNTIME_COLL_MAX_SKEW_MS, RUNTIME_TOPOLOGY_INTRA_LEAD_US.
- Debugging: enable NCCL_DEBUG=TRACE on a small reproduction cluster and collect dmesg on hosts.

Conclusion:
Softening strict collective start alignment appears to be a promising mitigation for p99 token latency caused by link-level variance and transient host stalls. The approach is low-risk if rollout is conservative, but requires close telemetry on memory footprint and error rates. Next: run a targeted 2-week soak on a non-critical Dedicated pool with telemetry gates and rollback automation.

Notes-to-self:
- Add concise one-pager for SOC/Support describing what to tell customers if they see p99 when feature is enabled.
- Cross-link this doc with the "priority lanes" kernel experiment (tickets referenced above) after we have 16-GPU results.

End of note.
